Project_Name: City Park Living Shorelines (Volusia County)
Project_Description: The City Parks Living Shorelines-City of Edgewater project is a result of a largescale Living Shorelines initiative which has been conducted throughout the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) over the past decade. FWC has partnered with regional entities (municipalities, Marine Discovery Center-MDC, University of Central Florida-UCF) to conduct Living Shorelines projects, sometimes using MEHRMA funding. Other regional entities (e.g., Florida Oceanographic Society, Brevard Zoo) have also played a role in these types of enhancements. As a result, the IRL restoration community has perfected techniques for improving IRL shorelines in terms of using natural products to secure erosion. The project is a partnership between FWC and the City of Edgewater. During 2016/17, the partners identified two city parks along Mosquito Lagoon in the IRL experiencing erosion. General conceptual plans were developed to secure the erosion through Living Shoreline designs. Living Shorelines emphasize the use of natural products such as native stone and plants as opposed to traditional hardening techniques such as seawalls. The funding provided by MEHRMA for the City Parks project was used to purchase native coquina rock which will be used along the park waterfront as breakwaters to reduce wave energy and promote sediment accretion and plant survivorship. The coquina and native plants provide habitat for aquatic organisms.
Partners: City of Edgewater

Project_Name: Don Pedro Island State Park Tidal Marsh Restoration (Charlotte County)
Project_Description:
Prior to state acquisition of Don Pedro Island State Park, dredged material from a canal adjacent to the park was placed
along the south park boundary creating an artificial berm that restricted natural hydrologic flows and wildlife access to the saltmarsh and mangrove habitats. The goal of this project was to restore historic tidal connections and flows to approximately 20 acres of saltmarsh and mangrove habitats. This was achieved by the removal of 2.79 acres of the dredge spoil along the 994 ft. canal bank. Locations where dredged material is removed is being replanted with native species found in the adjacent saltmarsh and mangrove/oyster communities, which will aid in shoreline stabilization and in enhancement of the habitats. This project increased tidal exchange on a north/south continuum with the waters of Lemon Bay, a state aquatic preserve and a portion of the Charlotte Harbor National Estuary focus area. The restored tidal connection and enhanced habitats will provide a nursery and foraging areas for a variety of wildlife species, including: juvenile fish, wading birds, manatees, invertebrates, and oysters. Also, this enhanced saltmarsh habitat will benefit the state threatened golden leather fern which is present in the marsh. This project is within a state park and is part of a larger effort to restore the previously disturbed area to its natural condition and function.
Partners: US Fish and Wildlife Service State Wildlife Grant Program (USFWS SWG), Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP)

Project_Name: East Greynolds Park Coastal Wetlands Restoration and Enhancement
Project_Description: East Greynolds Park is a Miami-Dade County park located in North Miami Beach. The park encompasses 43 acres, of which, approximately 33.4 acres are managed by the Miami-Dade Environmentally Endangered Lands Program (EEL). East Greynolds Park is located along the Oleta River Corridor and is situated on the western bank of Maule Lake – an old rock mining pit that is tidally connected to Biscayne Bay and Dumbfoundling Bay. The park contains a variety of habitats, which include subtropical hardwood hammock, mangrove wetlands, and exotic dominated upland and transitional wetland communities. The overall goal of this project was to remove exotic vegetation and restore appropriate wetland elevations. The project focused on an area of approximately 8.55 acres of red mangrove and transitional coastal wetland habitats located along the east and northeast portions of the park. The subject areas are dominated by non-native and invasive plants, such as Australian pine and Brazilian pepper, which have proliferated in disturbed areas where the placement of excess fill has altered historic wetland elevations and native soils. Restoration of these habitats improves both habitat and water quality within the Oleta River Corridor and Biscayne Bay, as well as providing critical coastal resilience to sea level rise along the densely urban landscape of southeast Florida.
Partners: Miami-Dade County, Frost Museum

Project_Name: FISH Preserve Coastal Resotration and Enhancement Phase III
Project_Description: Florida Institute for Saltwater Heritage (FISH) Preserve is a 100- acre publically-accessible community conservation property in the historic Village of Cortez, Manatee County. The project area includes tidal creek, mangroves, saltmarsh, and coastal hammock habitats. The purpose of this project is to restore tidal wetland function and enhance habitats for estuarine- dependent species. This project builds upon the success of two completed phases of restoration, continuing the planned control of exotic invasive plants, creation of tidal creeks, and planting of intertidal marsh with beneficial native grasses. This project involved engineering and design plan updates during 2018 and 2019, as well as development of specifications for construction. The project is fully shovel- ready for construction of Phase III during fiscal year 2019/2020. Additional project funding in FY18/19 was contributed by Sarasota Bay Estuary Program (SBEP), the project partner and permittee, through in-kind project management services. $284,000 in leveraged funds from the first two phases of the project were provided by SBEP, Southwest Florida Water Management District, and Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership.
Partners: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program (SBEP), Southwest Florida Water Management District (SWFWMD), Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership

Project_Name: Goffinsville Park Living Shoreline
Project_Description: Goffinsville Park is a popular park managed by Nassau County, within the Nassau River – St. Johns River Marshes Aquatic Preserve. The Park includes a playground, picnic area, restrooms, fishing pier, and public boat ramp. A living shoreline was completed in 2016 along approximately 200’ of shoreline on the western edge of the park. This project built on the success of the 2016 efforts by installing multiple non-plastic oyster restoration materials to serve as a wave break in front of the seawall, extending the existing living shoreline. This arrangement allows for side-by-side comparison of multiple oyster restoration materials, including CORE modules, Reefballs, and Reef Prisms. The project is intended to enhance estuarine habitat, improve water quality, and reduce erosion while engaging the public. Volunteers and citizen scientists were involved in the project via the Florida Master Naturalist Program, IFAS Extension opportunities, and the Florida Master Gardener Program. The Park now serves as a demonstration site for homeowners to physically view available material options when planning to install a living shoreline along their own waterfront property. High-quality educational signs displayed above the demonstration area outline the benefits of living shorelines and the specific materials utilized at the site. UF/IFAS Extension with Nassau County took the lead on this project, working closely with the UF Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience. FWC supported the effort through the purchase of oyster CORE modules, supplies to construct reef prisms, design and purchase of educational signs, as well as field support for monitoring and installation. In FY 18/19, $2,006 were spent on the project to purchase supplies. The remaining $4,245 was expended in FY 19/20 to cover additional supplies and signs. UF/IFAS Extension provided $22,841 of in-kind match through staff time (480 hours) and volunteer assistance (320 hours).
Partners: UF,IFAS

Project_Name: Harbor Branch Mangrove March Restoration (St. Lucie County)
Project_Description:
In 2010, the Marine and Estuarine Sub-section of FWC, in partnership with St. Lucie County, applied for and was awarded a $1M grant from the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) through their National Coastal Wetland Conservation Grant Program to implement a 178-acre wetland restoration project in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) system. The overarching goal of the restoration project was to conserve and restore tidal connectivity to 178 acres of impaired estuarine intertidal forested habitat (mangroves) that were impounded in the 1950’s and 1960’s for mosquito control. This was done by restoring hydrologic connectivity to the wetland through the stabilization of an existing but severely eroded dike and the installation of culverts to restore tidal exchange between the wetland and the IRL. FWC contracted St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District (SLC MCD), the project designer, to complete construction of this project. The project was successfully completed in February 2016 by stabilizing the dike and installing 18 culverts. The FY 17/18 MEHRMA award was originally intended to purchase and place limerock to reinforce priority shoreline areas to adequately protect the project perimeter from wind and wave action. Due to unexpected construction challenges and unanticipated additional expenses, the original project construction fell short of providing adequate stabilization of the culverts and the dike (on the IRL side). The addition of limerock was intended to provide extra security against future breaches of the dike or de-stabilization of culverts which would compromise the effective tidal exchange established by the original project. At the end of FY 16/17, MEHRMA funding became available and was used to purchase 300 cy of limerock that was stockpiled on site, to be placed when MEHRMA 17/18 funding became available. Prior to implementation of the FY 17/18 MEHRMA project, in September 2017, Hurricane Irma
passed over southern Florida and caused extensive damage to the dike. As a result, repairs and maintenance not previously planned were required. FEMA became a project partner and will ultimately reimburse St. Lucie County for materials that were purchased and placed to repair the dike and the road damaged by the storm. Following Irma, much of the stabilization work that was to be implemented by FWC, became part of the FEMA emergency repair project. Thus, MEHRMA funding was used only to place FWC purchased riprap on areas of the dike that were not impacted by Hurricane Irma, but were identified as needing reinforcement prior to Irma. Specifically, the riprap was placed around 18 culverts and on 150 linear feet of shoreline.
Funding_Program: National Coastal Wetland Conservation Grant Program
Partners: St. Lucie County

Project_Name: Highland Beach Mangrove Restoration (Palm Beach County)
Project_Description: The Highland Beach Mangrove Project consists of 24 acres of estuarine habitat, predominantly mangroves, divided into two parcels separated by a housing community, located in the Town of Highland Beach, in southern Palm Beach County. The mangrove areas are owned by Palm Beach County or are in private ownership and under conservation easements. The narrowness of the ICW and lack of a speed zone in the project area is causing severe erosion to the naturally existing mangroves. In fact, aerial imagery shows that since the 1940's, the shoreline in this area has receded shoreward over 60 feet. The purpose of this project was to preserve and enhance 17.6 acres of mangroves by installing a 1,700 linear foot (0.8 acre) limestone riprap breakwater. The limestone attenuates waves, reduces the effects of boat wakes, prevents scouring and protects seagrass beds from sedimentation in the project area. The rock serves as substrate  for the recruitment and colonization of oysters, sponges, and algae. The enhanced habitat provides nursery and foraging habitat for a variety of wildlife including juvenile fish, invertebrates, oysters, wading birds, manatees and juvenile green sea turtles.
Partners: Palm Beach County Department of Environmental Resources Management

Project_Name: Installation of Native Vegetation at FWC's Mosquito Lagoon Marine Enhancement Center (Volusia County)
Project_Description: This project is a supplement to a partner-based and NOAA grant funded restoration of saltmarsh on FWC property in New Smyrna Beach. The 5-acre restoration was conducted between July and November, 2014, with SJRWMD contractors conducting the excavation of ~45,000 cubic yards of fill. During August-November, 2014, native plants (roughly 17,000 plants; various brackish wetland species) were purchased using MEHRMA funds for the project at cost of $9052. The plants were installed by FWC staff and partners, mainly volunteers associated with MDC, the non-profit organization housed at the FWC property. Additional plants and supplies were provided as match and a total of 25,000 plants were installed at the site. In addition, MEHRMA funds were used to purchase sod to secure the excavated sand storage mountain created as a result of the project and to purchase French drain supplies to repair eroding areas along a shoreline stabilization demonstration area created as part of the project. Excavated spoil was used to create a publicly accessible mountain overlooking the created saltmarsh, a future building pad, and an amphitheater adjacent to the marsh.
Partners: NOAA’s Coastal Habitat Restoration program, St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD), Costa del Mar Inc., Marine Discovery Center Inc. (MDC), Brevard Zoo (BZ), City of New Smyrna Beach, USFWS

Project_Name: Jewell Cove Shoreline Restoration (Palm Beach County)
Project_Description: Jewell Cove is an 11.44 acre area that lies within the City of Lake Worth along the eastern shoreline of the Lake Worth Lagoon. The project area included an eroding shoreline, a maritime hammock dominated by exotics, and submerged lands. The purpose of this project was to remove exotic vegetation, protect the shoreline from erosion, and install native plants along 1,100 linear feet of shoreline. Limestone boulders, proven to be viable oyster reef habitat in this area, were installed to protect the shoreline and provide mangrove, Spartina, and oyster habitats. The boulders also add shoreline resilience in regards to climate change and sea level rise and enhance recreational fishing opportunities. Future components of the project, a shell rock pedestrian pathway through the hardwood hammock and an informational kiosk, will add public access and educational opportunities. Jewell Cove is part of a bigger project known as Old Bridge Park. Additional components of the Old Bridge Park project to which this funding did not contribute include repairing a failing seawall and installation of a shade shelter and day-use dock for the public for recreation and fishing. Kiosks and signs about the overall project will be installed to provide information to the public about the environmental benefits and the sponsors of the project. The Old Bridge Park project received additional funding from the Florida Inland Navigation District and from the FDEP through the 2014- 2015 General Appropriations Act program grant. The funding provided by MEHRMA for the Jewell Cove Shoreline portion of the project was used as match towards the FIND and FDEP grants for the Old Bridge Park project. When Old Bridge Park is complete, the total project costs (Old Bridge Park components and Jewell Cove components) are estimated to be approximately $764,000.
Partners: FDEP, Palm Beach County Department of Environmental Resources Management

Project_Name: Jones Pier living shoreline
Project_Description: The Jones Pier Conservation Area (JPCA) is part of the rich history of late 19th century/early 20th century settlement in Indian River County. In 1889, Seaborn Jones and his family homesteaded 160 acres on Orchid Island. Mr. Jones and his neighbors built the “Orchid-Narrows Road” which is now known as Jungle Trail (listed in 2003 on the National Register of Historic Places). The 16- acre JPCA that was purchased by the County in 2011 (including the docks) is part of this original homestead. The County acquired the site from the Jones’ family with assistance from the Florida Communities Trust (FCT). As part of the purchase, the County committed to implementing a management plan for the site that restores ecological value, while at the same time utilizes the existing buildings on the property for public access and display of educational and historical exhibits. To this end, the County has developed a Master Plan for the site that includes restoration/creation of wetlands on-site as well as a Living Shoreline. The improvements include the creation of a 2.8-acre high marsh community that will filter Lagoon waters (Fig. 1). High marsh is a rare resource in this portion of the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), and it is anticipated that this wetland will provide diverse habitat and improved water quality in proximity to the site. The construction of the high marsh is to be funded, in part, through a grant from the Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program (IRLNEP) with matching funds from the County. The discharge location for the high marsh wetland occurs within a section of shoreline where concrete and rubble were deposited historically to minimize erosion. There is minimal coverage by desirable shoreline vegetation, and very little potential habitat for wildlife. The entire 2.25-mile section of Jungle Trail that fronts the Lagoon is devoid of emergent herbaceous vegetation. MEHRMA funds provide for the construction of ~125 linear feet of functional living shoreline along Jungle trail, a highly visible section of the Indian River Lagoon. The living shoreline will function as the terminal section of the habitat and water quality improvement efforts on the JPCA. During FY 2018/19, MEHRMA funds were used to purchase the native coquina rock boulders which will be placed along the shoreline and coupled with native plants. The County also plans to incorporate extensive educational displays showcasing the importance of these types of habitats with respect to the ecology of the Lagoon environment.
Partners: Indian River County, IRLNEP

Project_Name: New Smyrna Beach Saltmarsh Restoration/Marsh Madness (Volusia County)
Project_Description: The Marsh Madness project is a result of a largescale saltmarsh restoration which was conducted on FWC property in New Smyrna Beach. The restoration (partially funded through MEHRMA) occurred in 2014 and the saltmarsh has been growing in terms of the spread of native plantings and the attraction of numerous species to the new habitat. FWC partnered with regional entities (Marine Discovery Center-MDC, University of Central Florida-UCF, and Volusia County School Board-VCSB) in order to survey the saltmarsh growth, species utilization, and various water quality parameters. The project is run out of FWC’s Mosquito Lagoon Marine Enhancement Center which houses MDC. During 2015/16, the partners created a region-wide biological sampling and surveying protocol of the new saltmarsh and reference areas by studying water quality, sediment elevation, various plant components, and use by animals (fish, invertebrates, birds) . To facilitate citizen science, citizens were trained to use the protocols and provided with the tools (eg, water quality testing kits) necessary. Biology teachers and students from the county AP programs were also trained in the field to use these data collection techniques. UCF conducted surveys at the new saltmarsh and reference sites to compare restoration techniques. FWRI conducted sediment sampling at various sites as part of a statewide wetland soil nutrient project. The partners also transplanted saltmarsh grasses from the new marsh to a recently restored one at a State Park in Ormond Beach. The funding provided by MEHRMA for the Marsh Madness project was used as match towards the funds and time provided by the partners. As a result, the program is now established to continue in the future as the partners contribute data to the newly-created database.
Main_Funding_Source: Marine Discovery Center-MDC, University of Central Florida-UCF, and Volusia County School Board-VCSB
Partners: FWRI, Marine Discovery Center-MDC, University of Central Florida-UCF, and Volusia County School Board-VCSB

Project_Name: Oleta River State Park Estuarine Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: This project will restore two remnant mangrove systems, in Oleta River State Park, in Miami-Dade County, that are currently experiencing mangrove die-off. These wetlands were impounded within the landscape during the large-scale dredging and filling associated with coastal development in the 1950s and have been stressed due to failure of hydrologic connections (culverts) to tidal flow. This project will restore the two die-off areas, totaling 26.7 acres of mangrove habitat, by re-establishing tidal flow through the installation and maintenance of culverts and removal of hydrologic barriers.
Funding_Program: US Fish and Wildlife Service State Wildlife Grant Program (USFWS SWG)
Partners: Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) Division of Recreation and Parks (DRP), US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) State Wildlife Grants Program (SWG), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Hurricane Irma Emergency Funds, Florida International University (FIU), Palm Beach Atlantic University (PBAU)

Project_Name: Oyster Reef and Seagrass Habitat Restoration in St. Andrew Bay (Bay County)
Project_Description: While St. Andrew Bay as a whole supports healthy seagrass habitat and high species diversity (~3,600 species; Keppner & Keppner 2001), the western arm of St. Andrew Bay known as West Bay has had a long history of anthropogenic impacts to seagrasses.  The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) has designated a seagrass restoration site just south of recent increases in seagrass coverage (Figure 1). Over the course of 2015-2019, the FWC installed approximately two hectares of oyster reef habitat along the deep edge of historic seagrass coverage. At its maximum extent (circa 1964), seagrasses extended from just waterward of mean low water (MLW) to approximately mean low, low water (MLLW; 4-feet NAVD88). Oyster reef habitat was installed to mitigate wind-driven wave energy, reduce suspended sediments, increase water filtration, and further facilitate both the natural recruitment of seagrasses and the expansion of transplanted seagrass beds. To better understand the restoration potential for seagrasses in West Bay, the FWC implemented a series of research studies looking at light availability, donor bed suitability, and transplanting methodology.
Partners: NA

Project_Name: Oyster Reef Restoration (Volusia County)
Project_Description: Brevard Zoo has teamed with UCF to restore oyster reefs in Mosquito Lagoon over the past few years. The reefs suffer from boat wakes piling live oysters above the intertidal zone, killing the oysters and creating “dead margins” of shell on once productive reefs. Volunteers assist by raking down the dead margins to intertidal elevations, and deploying weighted oyster mats on the affected reef areas. Once in place, oyster larvae quickly recruit to the shells and grow to make a functional reef system. The mats are created using oysters attached to mats by volunteers, including school groups and civic organizations. In this manner, over 75 reefs have been restored and secured in Mosquito Lagoon, Volusia County. UCF monitors the restored reef, tracking performance measures such as oyster recruitment, growth, and survivorship
Partners: Brevard Zoo - UCF

Project_Name: Restoration of Dragline-Ditched Saltmarsh in NE FL
Project_Description: The Flagler dragline-ditched saltmarsh restoration project is a result of a largescale restoration initiative which has been conducted throughout the east coast of Florida over the past two decades. FWC has partnered with regional entities (St. Johns River Water Management District, Volusia County) and a federal partner (USFWS) to conduct coastal wetland restoration, sometimes using MEHRMA funding. The USFWS provides funds through the National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grant Program (NCWCGP). Coastal wetlands in this region were greatly altered by the practice of dragline ditching during the mid-1900s as a mosquito control measure. The process left numerous ditches with adjacent spoil piles thereby reducing the marsh footprint. The original objective of this project was to restore more than 250 acres of dragline ditch-impacted wetlands on public lands in Volusia County. Following the restoration of 103 acres in Volusia during 2013-15, the secondary objective is to restore 96 acres of dragline ditch-impacted wetlands on public lands in Flagler County. Using the proven restoration technique, vegetation is cleared from the spoil area and placed in the adjacent ditch. This process avoids burning the plants and permanently sequesters the carbon they contain. Spoil material is moved to the side “fingers” of the ditch restoring marsh elevations or shoaling finger ditches. If additional material remains, the main ditch is narrowed. The area of the spoil pile and the newly-filled ditch are graded to the adjacent wetland elevation. This results in substantially more marsh area at coastal wetland elevation while still providing effective mosquito control.
Partners: St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD), US Fish and Wildlife Service State Wildlife Grant Program (USFWS SWG)

Project_Name: Restoring Mangrove Islands in Pine Island Sound
Project_Description: This project restored mangrove and oyster reef habitat for fish and wildlife Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Pine Island Sound using methods demonstrated to work effectively in the area. Pine Island Sound is characterized by extensive mangrove shorelines and mangrove islands, fringing oyster reefs, and shallow seagrass beds which serve as important feeding, breeding, and nursery habitats for fish and wildlife. Repeated hurricanes and sea level rise damaged and degraded habitats on and surrounding five islands managed by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as part of the Pine Island National Wildlife Refuge: Hemp Key, Bird Key, Benedict Key, Rat Key, and Cat Key. Restoration of resiliency and habitat function at these five islands is being achieved through planting of mangrove propagules, enhancement of oyster reefs, and structural and functional monitoring during this three-year project. Hemp Key is designated by FWC as a Critical Wildlife  Area because it supports a high density of nesting wading and diving birds. Pilot mangrove planting, oyster reef restoration, and initial monitoring were completed by Sanibel- Captiva Conservation Foundation (SCCF) staff and volunteers supported by a State Wildlife Grant (SWG) through USFWS. AHCR provided appropriation funding that was used deliver and stage 50 cubic yards of large fossil shell that was used in oyster reef enhancement. During subsequent grant years SCCF will continue mangrove and oyster restoration and monitoring.
Funding_Program: US Fish and Wildlife Service State Wildlife Grant Program (USFWS SWG)
Partners: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation (SCCF)

Project_Name: San Carlos Bay Oyster Reef Restoration
Project_Description: San Carlos Bay is a 10,000-acre waterbody between the mouth of the Caloosahatchee River, Sanibel Island, Pine Island, and the Gulf of Mexico. The project area included an oyster reef and adjacent submerged lands. The purpose of this project was to restore a large degraded oyster reef. This project built upon the success of two prior oyster reef restoration projects conducted by the Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation (SCCF) in both San Carlos Bay and nearby Tarpon Bay. This project employed the same restoration techniques used in the previous successful restorations. Fossilized oyster shell (approximately 700 yd3 of 4’’ shell) was added to the existing degraded reef to increase reef elevation and provide oyster colonization substrate over a one acre area. Additional project funding was contributed by the West Coast Inland Navigation District through the Lee County Natural Resources Department. To increase awareness of the importance of oyster reefs, SCCF held four volunteer oyster reef restoration events. Monitoring will be conducted by SCCF for 2 years following the guidelines in the Oyster Habitat Restoration Monitoring and Assessment Handbook (Baggett et al. 2014).
Partners: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation (SCCF), West Coast Inland Navigation District

Project_Name: Sarasota Bay Oyster Habitat Restoration Project (Manatee County)
Project_Description: The Sarasota Bay Oyster Habitat Restoration and Enhancement Project is located in the northern part of Sarasota Bay in Manatee County. The project site has intertidal and subtidal sandy bay bottom substrate and is surrounded by natural sloping shorelines which will allow for potential shoreward migration. The purpose of this project is to create four 20-foot-diameter oyster reef beds using approximately 34 tons of fossilized oyster shell. The habitat design of the oyster reef beds closely mimics the natural structure and functional elements of existing oyster habitat in Sarasota Bay. Each oyster reef bed is comprised of a continuous perimeter of bagged shell with loose shell material in the interior. The overall footprint of this project is approximately 1.2 acres of oyster habitat. This project was started during Fiscal Year 2015- 2016 as Marine and Estuarine Habitat Restoration, Monitoring and Assessment (MEHRMA) funds were used to purchase the 34 tons of fossilized oyster shell for $1,088.32. In addition, the Sarasota Bay Estuary Program (SBEP) funded and acquired all necessary permitting for this project. The remainder of this project was conducted during Fiscal Year 2016-2017, including purchasing of materials and construction of the oyster bags and oyster reef beds. SBEP’s volunteer program, Bay Guardians, assisted in the construction and filling of the oyster bags.
Partners: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program (SBEP)

Project_Name: Tarpon Cove Estuarine Habitat Restoration
Project_Description:
The Lake Worth Lagoon estuary in Palm Beach County (PBC) runs approximately 20 miles parallel to the southeast coastline of Florida. It is an urban estuary that has suffered extensive loss of estuarine habitats and degraded water quality due to human development activities over the past century. Approximately 81% of the lagoon’s shoreline is developed with seawalls associated with private residences and businesses. Dredge activities associated with development decades ago resulted in large benthic “holes” that now impair the Lagoon’s ecosystem. These “dredge holes” are typically well below grade, often anoxic, and generally do not support seagrass or wildlife. Additionally, canals that drain into the Lagoon have introduced fine, silty sediments that settle in these holes, hindering recruitment of seagrasses and diminishing water quality. The Tarpon Cove project will expand restoration efforts by filling in a deep dredge hole to restore and enhance important shallow estuarine seagrass habitat through the capping of anoxic, fine-grained organic sediments (i.e., muck). Capping the muck, by filling the hole, will allow for the natural recruitment of seagrasses, including Johnson’s seagrass (Halophila johnsonii), a federally threatened species, to naturally recruit. Additionally, the project will result in five intertidal islands consisting of mangrove, tidal saltmarsh, intertidal sand flat, and oyster reef habitats, along with a beach- nesting bird island. These islands are expected to support over 120 species of fish, 39 species of birds, and 14 state and/or federally listed species including West Indian manatee, Johnson’s sea grass, American oystercatcher and least tern. Other benefits of the project include downstream water-quality improvements, improved wildlife- and fisheries oriented recreational opportunities, increased protection of shorelines from coastal storms and flooding, and increased carbon sequestration capabilities, the latter of which contribute to resilience to the effects of climate change.
The final project, including all phases, will ultimately provide almost 40 acres of restored estuarine habitat.
Funding_Program: National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grant Program (NCWCGP)
Partners: Palm Beach County Department of Environmental Resources Management (PBC ERM), Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), USFWS State Wildlife Grant Program (SWG)

Project_Name: Tomoka State Park Living Shoreline Stablization
Project_Description: Tomoka State Park spans 2,000 acres in northern Volusia County, and is home to important historical, ecological, and cultural resources (Figure 1). The Park is located along a unique large estuarine basin, and provides opportunities for camping, fishing, boating, kayaking, wildlife viewing, and hiking. Numerous Native American shell middens and plantation-era artifacts are protected within the Park, however, segments of shoreline are severely eroding due to several strong storms and constant wave action from boat wakes. This project stabilized 1000 meters of shoreline along Tomoka State Park using ‘Living Shoreline’ principles. The Living Shoreline design consisted of mangroves (Rhizophora mangle, Avicennia germinans, and Laguncularia racemosa), smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora), and oyster shell bags. Living shoreline components were selected due to their natural occurrence in the region and were monitored for one year following installation. Vegetated shorelines and oyster reefs provide numerous benefits, including water filtration, nutrient cycling, and carbon sequestration. A combination of shoreline plants and oyster reefs trap sediment, allowing shorelines to stabilize and maintain their position. Living shorelines can naturally adjust to impacts of climate change such as sea level rise and increased storm activity, and preserve essential ecological functions  in the future. Local volunteers and students were heavily engaged in installing and monitoring the project.
Partners: Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program

Project_Name: Volusia Dragline Ditch Restoration (Volusia County)
Project_Description: Restoration of coastal saltmarsh wetlands in Volusia County began with an unusual machine - an amphibious excavator mounted on a pair of tracked pontoons. The low weight-bearing machine (less than 2 pounds per square inch) can float in water or move across wetland grasses without killing them. First, undesirable vegetation is cleared from a spoil area and placed in the adjacent ditch. This avoids the need to burn the plants and permanently sequesters the carbon they contain in the marsh sediment. Second, spoil material is moved to side “fingers” of the ditch. If additional material remains, the main ditch also is narrowed. After decades of soil compaction, the entire dragline ditched area cannot be filled. But the areas containing spoil piles and newly filled portions of ditches can be graded to the elevation of adjacent wetlands. The result? The area of vegetated coastal wetlands is roughly doubled. The amphibious machine is owned and operated by Volusia County. Grant funds for the project were provided through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Coastal Wetland Conservation Grant Program. Matching funds came from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and St. John’s Water Management District. From 2009 to 2012, 283 acres of coastal saltmarsh wetlands, including 140 acres returned to appropriate elevation, were restored in Volusia County at a cost of nearly $1.2 million.
Funding_Program: National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grant Program (NCWCGP)
Partners: St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD), NOAA, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS)

Project_Name: Warm Mineral Springs-Salt Creek restoration
Project_Description:
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) is working with partners to restore Warm Mineral Springs’ downstream run, which is
considered the most important natural manatee warm-water refuge along Florida’s southwest coast. Located in Sarasota County near the City of North Port, this project will improve warm-water access and habitat quality for the more than 100 Florida manatees that have been documented using Warm Mineral Springs Creek as a refuge during the winter months. Historical and current land use, bank erosion, sedimentation and invasive plants are degrading the quality of the creeks flowing from Warm Mineral Springs. The permitted project will include removal of some sediments from the spring run and stabilization of creek banks. While geographically distant from the Atlantic Coast Manatee Unusual Mortality Event (UME), this collaborative project directly benefits the Florida manatee population by improving critically important warm-water habitat.
Partners: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Sarasota County, The Nature Conservancy, Coastal and Heartland National Estuary Partnership (CHNEP), City of North Port, National Wildlife Federation (NFWF)
